solutions.check: 28 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Sacked Eurosceptic, that is to say, revolutionary

parts.note: Sir Bill Cash, veteran Tory Eurosceptic MP

explanation.surface: A Eurosceptic politician has been fired, and the clue spells out that he was a revolutionary.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill Cash was a long-serving Conservative MP famous for opposing the EU, so the surface's sacked Eurosceptic is a real type of Westminster figure.
explanation.definitionFit: A military word: an officer dismissed from the service in disgrace is cashiered, which extends to anyone sacked.

clue.text: Weeks spent on Democrat's debut — biased?

indicators.note: spent means used up and worn out, so the letters of the word are knocked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

indicators.note: a debut is a first appearance, so only the first letter is taken

parts.note: the word Democrat, of which only the opening letter is used

explanation.surface: After weeks of campaigning, a Democrat's first outing is accused of partisan slant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spent' rearranges WEEKS into SKEWE and 'debut' supplies D from Democrat's.
explanation.definitionFit: Skewed coverage or reasoning is distorted towards one side, which is what being biased means.

clue.text: Tender arse enclosed in raunchy fringes

parts.note: an arse, as an insult, is a contemptible person: a cur

indicators.note: the fringes of a word are its outside letters, like the fringe on a rug

parts.note: enc. is the abbreviation for enclosed, as at the foot of a letter

explanation.surface: A cheeky picture of a sore backside tucked inside racy frilly underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tender' wants to mean sore, next to 'arse'; it is money, as in legal tender. Arse as an insult for a person is British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Legal tender is the money a creditor must accept, so tender on its own stands for money in circulation.

clue.text: A bloody alternative route!

definitions.note: 'A bloody' stands for a bloody operation, a heart bypass
definitions.meaning: a bloody one, that is, heart surgery that reroutes the blood
a road built to carry traffic around a town

explanation.surface: An exasperated driver curses a detour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloody' looks like a driver's swear word; it is really the surgical sense, a heart operation being a bloody business.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a ring road around a town and the surgery that sends blood round a blocked artery.

clue.text: Modern art? Remove!

definitions.note: 'Modern art' stands for a kind of modern art, the non-representational kind
definitions.meaning: twentieth-century painting of shapes and colours rather than recognisable things
a formal verb for taking something out

explanation.surface: A gallery-goer faced with modern art demands it be taken away.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb, stressed on its second syllable, means to take out or extract, as in abstracting a summary from a paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: non-representational art, and a formal verb for extracting or taking away.

clue.text: Conservatives just started to get in correct order?

indicators.note: only the start of Conservatives is used, its first letter

explanation.surface: The Conservatives, barely begun, are trying to get into proper order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Correct order' reads as one phrase but splits: correct is EDIT, order is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a decree issued by an authority is an order in the commanding sense, not the tidy one.

clue.text: What some UK cities face, as reckless extreme wings of party turn back

indicators.note: reckless means wild and careless, so the letters are thrown into disorder
the extreme wings of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: the word party, of which only the ends are kept
taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Councils face ruin as both fringes of a political party demand a U-turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extreme wings of' gives PY from party, and 'reckless' mixes those two letters with TURN BACK. 'turn back' reads like an instruction to reverse, but it is only anagram material.
explanation.definitionFit: Several UK city councils, such as Birmingham, have issued section 114 notices, effectively declaring themselves insolvent.

clue.text: European leader replaced with time (depression)

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, and that letter is swapped for another

parts.note: a French person is a European, so French serves here

explanation.surface: A European leader is ousted and replaced, causing a slump in mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader replaced with' swaps the F at the head of FRENCH for T from time. The surface suggests a political leader; it is just a first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A trench is a long narrow ditch, a depression dug into the ground.

clue.text: Wait — presidential candidate name to be taken off!

indicators.note: a name taken off a list or ballot is removed, so the letter for name goes

parts.note: the Democrat who stood aside as candidate in 2024
N = name; this letter is removed

explanation.surface: A plea to pause while a presidential candidate's name is struck off the ballot.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls Joe Biden standing down in 2024, which is exactly what the wordplay does to his name: BIDEN loses N.
explanation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned verb for staying or waiting, surviving mostly in the idiom about biding one's time.

clue.text: One who reveals broadcaster takes heroin

parts.note: a sower broadcasts seed, scattering it by hand

explanation.surface: A whistleblower exposes a broadcaster's heroin use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcaster' suggests the BBC; its older sense is scattering seed, so a broadcaster is a sower. Read the answer as show-er, not the rain.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossword-only sense: the verb show plus -er, one who shows, rather than the rain or the wash.

clue.text: Nigel (as Tice?) able to endure a stretch inside

indicators.note: the answer lies inside the run of letters

explanation.surface: Nigel Farage, standing in for Richard Tice, could survive a spell in prison.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Tice is Farage's Reform UK deputy. 'A stretch' sounds like jail time, but here it is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: material that can be pulled out and spring back without breaking.

clue.text: (& 22ac.) Useless wanker is late meeting court date

explanation.surface: A useless tosser turns up late for his day in court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' and 'date' look like a legal appointment, but court is the romantic verb and date is only its abbreviation. The answer runs on into 22 across.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom from forestry: branches that bear nothing, applied to staff who contribute nothing to an organisation.

clue.text: Capital is in a mess: company needs to be incorporated

indicators.note: to be incorporated is to be taken into a body, so these letters sit within the jumble
a mess is a jumble, so the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A capital city is in chaos and a firm must be formally registered there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mess' turns IS IN A into NISIA, and 'needs to be incorporated' takes CO into it. 'incorporated' fits the business picture, but here it means put inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicosia is the capital city of Cyprus, divided between the Greek and Turkish communities.

clue.text: "Grass currently playing well," TV presenter

parts.note: in form = playing well at the moment
Ant McPartlin, of the TV duo Ant and Dec

explanation.surface: A TV presenter praises someone called Grass for a good run of form.
explanation.walkthrough: Ant and Dec are Britain's best-known TV presenting duo.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang: a grass is someone who tells the police about criminals, from rhyming slang grasshopper for copper.

clue.text: Gives away drawers after live introduction

indicators.note: after means following in sequence, so the drawers follow the word for live
an introduction is what comes first, so the word for live opens the answer

parts.note: sliding drawers in a cabinet are trays

explanation.surface: Someone hands over a chest of drawers after a live launch event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawers' suggests furniture or knickers; the trays inside a cabinet are the letters needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving away a secret or a friend is the treacherous sense; it can also mean simply revealing, as a blush does.

clue.text: "English taken in by Archer's falsification" : investigate

indicators.note: falsifying the letters of ARCHERS rearranges them

explanation.surface: A call to investigate English deceived by Jeffrey Archer's lies.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeffrey Archer, novelist and Tory peer, was jailed for perjury, so 'falsification' fits his name.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as a verb: to study a subject closely to establish facts.

clue.text: Distant object, not hard, acting as a windbreaker

explanation.surface: A remote, soft object is being used as a screen against the wind.
explanation.walkthrough: A windbreaker sounds like a screen on the beach; here it is someone breaking wind.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic twist on the idiom break wind: a windbreaker is taken literally as one who breaks wind.

clue.text: Everything associated with Rees-Mogg's position in the party is OK?

parts.note: Jacob Rees-Mogg sits on the right of the Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A sardonic question whether everything to do with Rees-Mogg's place in the party is fine.
explanation.walkthrough: Jacob Rees-Mogg, the Conservative MP and minister, is a figurehead of the party's right wing.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both are everyday words for satisfactory or acceptable, and the question mark fits the enquiring sense.

clue.text: Draw produces Sunak supporter, say, harbouring glimmer (of hope?)

parts.note: a ray of hope is a glimmer

explanation.surface: A contest ends in a draw, leaving a Sunak supporter clinging to a glimmer of hope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw' looks like a tied result or a noun; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The stick of coloured wax doubles as a verb: to make a picture with one.

clue.text: More than one cut by the state

explanation.surface: More than one thing has been cut by the government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The state' reads as government cuts; it is a US state abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a determiner for a number above one but not many.

clue.text: Naive move to acquire new capital

indicators.note: the letters of NAIVE move about

explanation.surface: A naive plan to buy new capital, as in funds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' again suggests money; it is a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Austria's seat of government on the Danube.

clue.text: see 12ac.
Evasive politician's words he might have to eat?

definitions.note: 'he might have to eat' stands for something one eats, a noun
definitions.meaning: long-winded talk that avoids saying anything definite

explanation.surface: A politician who dodged questions may end up eating his words.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface plays on eating one's words: the politician's evasive talk can also be a breakfast item.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: wordy talk with no substance, and the batter cake cooked in a gridded iron.

clue.text: Technique offering an opportunity to get your leg over, it's said

indicators.note: what is said is heard rather than read, so the word only has to sound right

parts.words: offering an opportunity to get your leg over
parts.note: a stile is a step for climbing over a fence

explanation.surface: A technique for getting lucky in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get your leg over' is British slang for having sex; here it means swinging a leg over the steps set into a field fence.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a characteristic manner of doing something, as in a swimmer's stroke or a writer's voice.

clue.text: Get Yard organised? Disaster!

indicators.note: the letters are organised into a new order

explanation.surface: A cry to sort out Scotland Yard, which is a disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: The Yard is Scotland Yard, London's Metropolitan Police headquarters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a calamitous event, borrowing the name of the drama that ends in catastrophe.

clue.text: Intelligence reduced May's dubious shame

indicators.note: reduced means cut short, so the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: info is short for information, which is intelligence in the spying sense

indicators.note: dubious means questionable or shady, so the name's letters are put in another order

parts.note: Theresa May, former Prime Minister; the 's stands for is

explanation.surface: Diminished intelligence under Theresa May is called a dubious disgrace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reduced' cuts INFO to INF, and 'dubious' rearranges MAY into AMY. Theresa May was the UK Prime Minister from 2016 to 2019.
explanation.definitionFit: Infamy is notoriety for bad deeds, a public disgrace or dishonour.

clue.text: Political alliance head: "Keir's first to go!"

indicators.note: to go means to leave, so that letter leaves the word for head

parts.note: block is slang for head, as in knock your block off

explanation.surface: An alliance leader demands that Keir Starmer be first out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' looks like the leader of the alliance; it is the slang for the skull.
explanation.definitionFit: Borrowed from French: a group of parties or nations voting or acting together, as in the Eastern one.

clue.text: Offhand Macron's negative election loser breaks into song

parts.note: Al Gore, who lost the 2000 US presidential election

explanation.surface: Macron's casual 'non' as a defeated candidate bursts into song.
explanation.walkthrough: Macron is French, so his no is NON.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from French: coolly unconcerned, casual in manner.
